opus-5.5.text:
I think posing a good conjecture is genuinely one of the hardest things in mathematics, and in some ways harder than proving things. A proof is a well-defined target: you know what you're trying to show, and you can check whether you've done it. With a conjecture there's no such checklist. You're making a bet about what's true before anyone knows, and the bet has to be interesting.

A good conjecture has a few qualities that pull against each other. It has to be plausibly true, so you need some evidence, whether computational data, special cases, or an analogy with a neighboring area. But it can't be so obviously true that it's trivial, and it can't be so wild that nobody knows where to start. The best conjectures sit right at the edge of what the community can reach. They feel just out of grasp, and trying to prove them forces you to invent new tools. Think of how much mathematics came out of people working on the Riemann Hypothesis or the Langlands program. The conjecture itself became a kind of organizing principle for a whole field.

There's also a taste component that's hard to articulate. Experienced mathematicians develop an intuition for which patterns are "structural" and which are coincidences. You can look at a sequence of numbers and find a hundred patterns, but most of them will break at the next term or won't connect to anything deeper. Knowing which pattern points to some hidden structure, that's the art. And honestly, a lot of that taste comes from years of failed guesses.

That's part of why I find it exciting to think about how machines could participate in this. Computers have long been great at generating data and spotting candidate patterns. The open question is whether we can build systems that don't just find patterns but judge which ones are worth pursuing, and then actually try to prove them in a verifiable way. If you combine large-scale exploration with formal verification, you get a loop: propose, test, attempt a proof, learn from the failure, refine. Human mathematicians do this loop in their heads. Making it explicit and scalable could change how quickly we move through that space of ideas.

But I'd say the human sense of what's *meaningful*, what connects to the questions we care about, is still the scarce resource. Generating conjectures is easy. Generating good ones is very, very hard.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think posing a good conjecture is harder than proving one, and I don't think that's a contrarian take anymore. When you're proving something, the target is fixed. You know what success looks like. You can fail a hundred times and still know exactly what you're aiming at. When you're posing a conjecture, you don't even know if the thing you're reaching for exists.

What makes it hard is that a good conjecture has to sit in a very narrow band. If it's too easy, it's a homework problem, nobody cares. If it's too hard, or too vague, it's not a conjecture, it's a wish. The great ones, like the Riemann hypothesis or the Langlands program, are precise enough to be checkable but deep enough that attacking them forces you to build entirely new machinery. That's the real test for me. Does trying to prove it generate mathematics on the way, even if you fail?

And the part people underestimate is taste. You need to have seen enough examples that you can feel when a pattern is real versus when it's a coincidence of small numbers. Mathematicians are very good at getting fooled by the first few cases. So a lot of posing a conjecture is actually computing, playing with examples, pushing until something either breaks or refuses to break. When something refuses to break for reasons you can't articulate, that's usually the signal.

This is actually one of the things I think about a lot with AI and math. Current systems are getting genuinely good at the proving side, given a well-posed statement. But asking the right question, deciding which of a thousand true statements is the one worth caring about, that's still deeply human right now. It requires a sense of what the field needs, what would unlock other things. I'm not sure that gap is permanent, but it's the gap I find most interesting.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s quite difficult, because you’re trying to find a statement that is both plausible and interesting. You can look at examples and notice a pattern, but it’s not always clear whether that pattern reflects something deeper or whether you just haven’t found the counterexample yet.

And there’s a balance: if your conjecture is too cautious, it might not tell you very much; if it’s too ambitious, you might have very little reason to believe it. Often, trying to prove something helps you formulate the conjecture itself. You discover which assumptions matter, where the argument breaks down, and what the right statement might be. So I think posing the question and solving it are much more intertwined than they can appear.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s very difficult. A good conjecture has to balance being ambitious with being grounded in evidence. You want it to capture something deeper than the examples you’ve checked, but you also want a reason to believe it’s true. Often, the hard part is figuring out what the right statement should be—what assumptions you need, and which details are actually essential. Trying to prove it, failing, and finding counterexamples can all help you get there.
